title: Ex parte Albert Levitt
lead: A citizen and Supreme Court bar member challenges Hugo Black’s appointment, but his shared public interest does not entitle him to obtain a constitutional merits decision.

actors.name: Albert Levitt
actors.role: Pro se movant, citizen and member of the Supreme Court bar.

actors.name: Justice Hugo Black
actors.role: Associate Justice whose eligibility and appointment Levitt sought to challenge.

proceedings: Levitt requested leave to file an original petition demanding that Black show cause for serving.
The Supreme Court denied leave to file on October 11, 1937.
limits: The short order does not adjudicate appointment validity or recite the factual basis of the emoluments objection. Black did not participate, and the volume records Cardozo’s illness-related absence during this period. There is no recorded separate opinion.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Levitt asks the Court to examine Black’s right to serve
paragraphs: Albert Levitt appeared without counsel and asked the Supreme Court for leave to file an original petition concerning Justice Hugo Black. The proposed petition would require Black to show cause why he should be permitted to serve as an Associate Justice.

Levitt asserted that the President’s appointment and the Senate’s confirmation were void. He invoked the constitutional ineligibility provision in Article I, § 6, clause 2, and argued that there was no vacancy to which Black could lawfully have been appointed.

sections.title: The papers reveal only interests shared with the public
sections.cue: Why did the constitutional allegations not by themselves secure a hearing?
paragraphs: Levitt’s papers disclosed no personal interest beyond his status as a citizen and a member of the Court’s bar. The Court treated those interests as insufficient to invoke judicial power to determine the validity of legislative or executive action.

The seriousness of an alleged structural constitutional defect did not establish that Levitt had personally suffered an injury or faced one immediately. His proposed challenge therefore failed before the Court reached whether Black’s appointment was valid.

sections.title: The order requires a direct injury or immediate threat
sections.cue: What distinction governed access to adjudication?
paragraphs: The Court required an individual bringing such a challenge to show a direct injury already sustained or immediately threatened by the disputed action. A general interest common to the public did not meet that requirement. Its short order cited earlier decisions in support without offering additional analysis of the appointment’s constitutional merits.
That reasoning did not foreclose every appointment challenge by a properly injured litigant. It resolved the inadequacy of the interest asserted by this movant.

sections.title: Leave to file is denied without a ruling sustaining the appointment
sections.cue: Who participated, and what exactly did the Court do?
paragraphs: On October 11, 1937, the Court’s unsigned per curiam order denied Levitt’s motion for leave to file. It did not issue the requested show-cause order, remove Black, or uphold his appointment on the constitutional merits. No dissent or separate opinion is recorded.

The volume’s participation note excludes Black from consideration and decision of orders announced October 11 or earlier. It also records Justice Cardozo’s illness-related absence during this period, apart from a later December 10 session. This was therefore not a nine-Justice judgment deciding the constitutional objection.

sources.pinpoint: Exact action and participation note; 302 U.S. 633–634
